title: Two Sum and Three Sum
candidate_brief: Given an integer array nums and a target, return the indices of two numbers that sum to the target. Exactly one solution exists, and the same element cannot be used twice.
prompt: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. You may assume exactly one solution exists and you may not use the same element twice. As a follow-up: given an array nums, return all unique triplets [a, b, c] such that a + b + c == 0 (3-Sum), with no duplicate triplets in the result.
blurb: The gateway hashing problem — a one-pass hash map for Two Sum, generalized to the sort + two-pointer sweep of 3-Sum.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Clarifies whether the array is sorted, whether indices or values are returned, whether duplicates exist, and (for 3-Sum) that TRIPLET values must be unique, not index tuples.

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Assess a correct approach and justified efficiency for the disclosed requirements; accept equivalent alternatives. Reference examples, not mandatory algorithms: For Two Sum reaches the one-pass hash map storing value->index and looking up target-x; recognizes the O(n^2) nested loop as the naive baseline. For 3-Sum reaches sort + fix one element + two-pointer, and connects it back to Two Sum.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Judge actual outputs and invariants of the chosen approach, crediting valid corrections. The following checks apply to the illustrated implementation, not every valid solution: Two Sum: checks the complement is already in the map before inserting so an element isn't used twice. 3-Sum: skips duplicate values for the fixed index AND for both pointers after a match to avoid duplicate triplets; moves both pointers only on a hit.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: Verify the time and space analysis of the actual implementation. Preserve disclosed performance requirements; these reference figures do not introduce hidden bounds or mandate an algorithm: Two Sum O(n) time / O(n) space with the hash map, vs O(n^2)/O(1) brute force or O(n log n) sorting plus two pointers, preserving original indices in value-index pairs with O(n) auxiliary space. 3-Sum O(n^2) time / O(1) or O(n) space.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Assess readability, appropriate structure and avoidable duplication in the chosen solution. These are illustrative implementation choices, not required forms: Two Sum is a tight single loop; 3-Sum factors the inner two-pointer scan cleanly and handles the duplicate-skipping with readable while-loops rather than tangled conditionals.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Empty/size<2 arrays, negatives, a value that is exactly half the target appearing once vs twice, all zeros for 3-Sum, fewer than 3 elements, no valid triplet.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Tests the duplicate-value cases explicitly (e.g. [0,0,0], [-1,-1,2]) rather than only a happy path, and verifies no duplicate triplets are emitted.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Assess whether the candidate explains the decisions and invariants of their own approach, without requiring an algorithm name or a prescribed order. Reference-specific explanation examples: Explains why the complement-check order matters, and why sorting enables the two-pointer sweep in the follow-up.

constraints: Two Sum: 2 <= nums.length <= 10^4, -10^9 <= nums[i], target <= 10^9, exactly one valid answer
3-Sum answer must contain no duplicate triplets; order of triplets and of values within a triplet does not matter

examples.explanation: nums[0] + nums[1] = 2 + 7 = 9, so the indices are 0 and 1.
The same value appears twice at different indices; the complement of the second 3 is the first 3, already in the map.
After sorting to [-4,-1,-1,0,1,2], the two distinct zero-sum triplets are found; the duplicate -1 is skipped so [-1,0,1] is not emitted twice.

test_cases.expected: [1,2] — must not pick index 0 twice; 3+3 is invalid, 2+4=6
[[0,0,0]] — a single triplet despite four zeros; duplicate-skip prevents repeats
[[-2,0,2],[-2,1,1]] — both valid, second uses the repeated 1s legitimately

reference.optimal_space: Two Sum O(n) for the hash map; 3-Sum O(1) beyond the output (sort in place) or O(n) if the sort is not in place

approaches.name: brute force (nested loops)
approaches.idea: Two Sum: for every i, scan every j>i checking nums[i]+nums[j]==target. 3-Sum: three nested loops over all index triples plus a set to dedupe. Straightforward, no extra insight, but quadratic/cubic.
approaches.space: O(1) (or O(triplets) for the dedupe set)

approaches.name: optimal Two Sum: one-pass hash map
approaches.idea: Iterate once. For each x=nums[i], compute need=target-x. If need is already a key in the map, return [map[need], i]. Otherwise store map[x]=i and continue. Checking BEFORE inserting guarantees the two indices are distinct, and the single pass is what makes it O(n).

approaches.name: sort + two-pointer (preserve indices for Two Sum; value-based 3-Sum)
approaches.idea: Sort. For Two-Sum-by-value, walk a left and right pointer inward: if sum<target move left up, if sum>target move right down, else record. Sorting bare values loses original positions, but sorting (value, original-index) pairs is a valid Two Sum approach with O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. Sorting values alone can use O(1) extra storage apart from the sorting implementation when values rather than original indices are wanted. 3-Sum reuses it: sort, then for each index i (skipping duplicate nums[i]), run the two-pointer sweep on the subarray to its right targeting -nums[i], skipping duplicate values on both pointers after each hit.
approaches.space: O(n) to preserve original indices for Two Sum; 3-Sum auxiliary space depends on the sorting implementation

follow_ups: Return VALUES instead of indices — now the sort + two-pointer approach becomes attractive (O(1) extra space).
3-Sum (above): all unique triplets summing to 0 — the canonical generalization.
3-Sum Closest: return the triplet sum nearest to target; track the best absolute difference during the same sweep.
4-Sum / k-Sum: recurse — fix one element and reduce to (k-1)-Sum, bottoming out at the two-pointer Two-Sum; O(n^(k-1)).
Two Sum on a sorted input stream / with duplicates counted, or Two Sum III where add() and find() are separate online operations.
reference.reference_solution:
twoSum(nums, target): seen = {}  // value -> index. for i, x in enumerate(nums): need = target - x; if need in seen: return [seen[need], i]; seen[x] = i. return []  // per constraints, unreachable. The check-before-insert order is the correctness crux: it prevents using nums[i] as both operands and it returns the earliest valid pair.

threeSum(nums): sort(nums); res = []; n = len(nums). for i in range(n-2): if nums[i] > 0: break  // sorted, no positive lead can sum to 0. if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue  // skip duplicate anchor. lo = i+1; hi = n-1. while lo < hi: s = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi]; if s < 0: lo += 1; elif s > 0: hi -= 1; else: res.append([nums[i], nums[lo], nums[hi]]); lo += 1; hi -= 1; while lo < hi and nums[lo] == nums[lo-1]: lo += 1; while lo < hi and nums[hi] == nums[hi+1]: hi -= 1. return res. Three independent duplicate skips (anchor, and both pointers after a hit) are what keep triplets unique without a hash set.
pitfalls: Two Sum: inserting into the map before checking the complement, which can match an element with itself.
3-Sum: forgetting to skip duplicate anchor values, producing repeated triplets.
3-Sum: skipping duplicates on only one pointer, or advancing only one pointer on a hit (infinite loop / missed pairs).
Using a hash-set dedupe on triplets as a crutch instead of the ordered skip — works but O(n) extra space and hides understanding.
Returning indices from the sorted 3-Sum when the original indices were required.

interviewer_notes: Let the candidate finish their reasoning and any workspace changes before a focused follow-up. Ask only about a material unresolved issue, then return the floor. Let the candidate complete Two Sum before introducing the authored Three Sum variant. Assess correctness and justified complexity without steering from a double loop to a hash map. nums=[3,3], target=6 can test distinct-index behavior after their own testing. For Three Sum, assess duplicate handling and complexity; [0,0,0,0] is a useful completed-solution test. Sorting and two pointers are private reference techniques, not hints to provide during a pause. Three Sum Closest or k-Sum is optional only if useful time remains after the current work is complete.
